column2: And Hermes of Cyllene was calling out the spirits
of the suitors; and he held in his hands the wand,
fair, golden, with which he charms the eyes of the men
whom he wishes, and others again he wakes even from sleep;
with this he led them, rousing them, and they followed gibbering.
And as bats in the depth of a wondrous cave
flit gibbering, when one has fallen
from the cluster from the rock, and they cling to one another,
so they went together gibbering; and before them led
Hermes the Helper along the mouldy paths.
They passed the streams of Oceanus and the White Rock,
and past the gates of the Sun and the district of dreams
they went; and soon they came to the asphodel meadow,
where the spirits dwell, the phantoms of the dead.
And they found the spirit of Achilles, son of Peleus,
and of Patroclus and of blameless Antilochus
and of Ajax, who was the best in form and figure
of the other Danaans after the blameless son of Peleus.
So these were gathered about him; and nearby
came the spirit of Agamemnon, son of Atreus,
grieving; and around him were gathered others, all who with him
in the house of Aegisthus died and met their fate.
To him first the spirit of the son of Peleus spoke:

Son of Atreus, we used to say that to thunder-delighting Zeus
25	you were dear above all heroes all your days,
26	because you ruled over many and mighty men
27	in the land of the Trojans, where we Achaeans suffered pains.
28	And yet to you too early was to stand by
29	deadly fate, which no one avoids who is born.
30	Would that, enjoying the honour which you ruled with,
31	you had met death and fate in the land of the Trojans;
32	then all the Achaeans would have made you a tomb,
33	and you would have won great fame also for your son hereafter;
34	but now it was fated that you be taken by a most piteous death.
Then the spirit of the son of Atreus answered him:

Happy son of Peleus, Achilles like the gods,
37	who died at Troy far from Argos; and around you others
38	were killed, the best sons of the Trojans and Achaeans,
39	fighting over you; and you in the whirl of dust
40	lay mighty in your mightiness, forgetful of horsemanship.
41	And we fought all day long; and we would never at all
42	have ceased from the battle, had not Zeus stopped us with a storm.
43	But when we had carried you to the ships out of the battle,
44	we laid you on a bier, having cleansed your fair skin
45	with warm water and oil; and around you many
46	hot tears the Danaans shed and cut their hair.
47	And your mother came from the sea with the immortal sea-nymphs
48	hearing the news; and a cry arose over the sea,
49	marvellous, and trembling seized all the Achaeans;
50	and they would have leapt up and gone to the hollow ships,
51	had not a man held them back who knew many things of old,
52	Nestor, whose counsel had appeared best also before;
53	he, thinking well for them, made a speech and said:
54	'Hold, Argives, do not flee, young men of the Achaeans;
55	this is his mother coming from the sea with the immortal sea-nymphs
56	to meet her dead son.'
57	So he spoke, and the great-hearted Achaeans stopped their fear.
58	And around you stood the daughters of the Old Man of the Sea
59	piteously lamenting, and put immortal clothes about you.
60	And the Muses, nine in all, answering one another with fair voice,
61	sang the dirge; there you would not have seen one of the Argives
62	without tears; so the clear-voiced Muse moved them.
63	Seventeen days alike by night and day
64	we mourned you, the immortal gods and mortal men;
65	on the eighteenth we gave you to the fire, and around you many
66	very fat sheep we slaughtered and curved-horned oxen.
67	And you burned in the clothing of the gods and much oil
68	and sweet honey; and many Achaean heroes
69	moved in arms round the pyre as you burned,
70	foot-soldiers and horsemen; and a great din arose.
71	But when the flame of Hephaestus had consumed you,
72	at dawn we gathered your white bones, Achilles,
73	in unmixed wine and oil; and your mother gave
74	a golden two-handled urn; and she said it was a gift
75	of Dionysus, and the work of far-famed Hephaestus.
76	In this lie your white bones, shining Achilles,
77	mixed with those of dead Patroclus, son of Menoetius,
78	and apart those of Antilochus, whom you honoured above all
79	the other comrades, after the dead Patroclus.
80	And around them then a great and blameless tomb
81	we heaped, the sacred host of Argive spearmen,
82	on a projecting headland, on the broad Hellespont,
83	that it might be seen from far from the sea by men
84	who are now born and who shall be hereafter.
85	And your mother, having asked the gods, set very beautiful prizes
86	in the midst of the contest for the best of the Achaeans.
87	Already you have been present at the funeral of many men,
88	heroes, when a king has died
89	and the young men gird themselves and prepare the contests;
90	but those you would most have marvelled at in your heart,
91	such very beautiful prizes as the goddess set for you,
92	silver-footed Thetis; for you were very dear to the gods.
93	So not even dead did you lose your name, but always for you
94	among all men there will be good fame, Achilles.
95	But what pleasure is this to me, since I wound up the war?
96	For on my homecoming Zeus devised a woeful destruction
97	for me by the hands of Aegisthus and my accursed wife.
So they spoke such things to one another,
and near them came the Guide, the slayer of Argus,
leading down the spirits of the suitors, subdued by Odysseus;
and the two, amazed, went straight to them when they saw them.
And the spirit of Agamemnon, son of Atreus, knew
the dear son of Melaneus, famous Amphimedon;
for he was his guest-friend, living in a house in Ithaca.
To him first the spirit of the son of Atreus spoke:

Amphimedon, what has happened to you that you have gone beneath the dark earth,
107	all picked men and of one age? Nor otherwise
108	could one by choosing select the best men in a city.
109	Did Poseidon subdue you in your ships,
110	rousing grievous winds and long waves?
111	Or did hostile men harm you on dry land
112	cutting off cattle and fair flocks of sheep,
113	or fighting for a city and for women?
114	Tell me, who ask; I claim to be your guest-friend.
115	Do you not remember when I went to your house there,
116	to urge Odysseus with godlike Menelaus
117	to follow to Ilium on the well-benched ships?
118	In a full month we crossed all the broad sea,
119	hardly persuading Odysseus, sacker of cities.
Then the spirit of Amphimedon answered him:

Most glorious son of Atreus, lord of men, Agamemnon,
122	I remember all this, Zeus-nurtured, as you say;
123	and I shall tell you everything well and truly,
124	the evil end of our death, how it came about.
125	We were wooing the wife of Odysseus, long gone;
126	and she neither refused the hateful marriage nor made an end of it,
127	devising for us death and black fate,
128	but this other guile she pondered in her mind:
129	setting up a great loom in the halls she wove,
130	a fine and ample cloth; and at once she said to us:
131	'Young men, my suitors, since godly Odysseus is dead,
132	wait, though eager for my marriage, until I finish
133	the cloth, that my threads not perish for nothing,
134	a shroud for the hero Laertes, against the time when
135	the deadly fate of long-lasting death takes him,
136	lest any of the Achaean women in the district blame me,
137	if he lies without a shroud, who had won so much.'
138	So she spoke, and our proud spirit was persuaded.
139	Then by day she wove the great loom,
140	but at night she unravelled it, when she had set torches by.
141	So for three years she went unnoticed by guile and persuaded the Achaeans;
142	but when the fourth year came and the seasons rolled on,
143	as the months waned, and many days were fulfilled,
144	then one of the women, who knew it clearly, told us,
145	and we found her unravelling the splendid loom.
146	So she finished it, and unwillingly, under compulsion.
147	When she showed the cloth, having woven the great loom
148	and washed it, shining like the sun or the moon,
149	then some evil god brought Odysseus from somewhere
150	to the edge of the farm, where the swineherd had his dwelling.
151	There came the dear son of godly Odysseus,
152	coming from sandy Pylos in a black ship;
153	and the two, devising an evil death for the suitors,
154	came to the famous town, Odysseus
155	later, but Telemachus led the way before.
156	The swineherd led him wearing bad clothes on his body,
157	like a wretched beggar and an old man,
158	leaning on a staff; and he wore miserable clothes on his body;
159	and none of us could recognise who he was,
160	appearing suddenly, not even those who were older,
161	but we assailed him with evil words and missiles.
162	But he for a time endured in his own halls
163	being pelted and abused with an enduring heart;
164	but when the mind of aegis-bearing Zeus roused him,
165	with Telemachus he took up the very beautiful arms
166	and laid them in the chamber and shot the bolts,
167	and in his great craftiness he bade his wife
168	set the bow for the suitors and the grey iron,
169	for us ill-fated, as prizes and the beginning of slaughter.
170	And none of us could string the cord
171	of the strong bow, but we were far short.
172	But when the great bow came into the hands of Odysseus,
173	then we all shouted with words
174	that they not give him the bow, however much he spoke;
175	but Telemachus alone urged and bade him.
176	And he took it in his hand, the much-enduring godly Odysseus,
177	and easily strung the bow, and shot through the iron,
178	and went and stood on the threshold, and poured out the swift arrows
179	looking dreadfully about, and hit Antinous the king.
180	And then at the others he shot his grievous shafts,
181	aiming straight; and they fell thick one by one.
182	And it was plain that some god was their helper;
183	for at once through the house, following in their fury,
184	they killed turning this way and that; and an ugly groan arose
185	from the heads being struck, and all the floor ran with blood.
186	So we perished, Agamemnon, whose bodies even now
187	lie uncared for in the halls of Odysseus;
188	for their friends in the house of each do not yet know,
189	who, washing the black blood from the wounds,
190	would lay them out and lament; for that is the due of the dead.
Then the spirit of the son of Atreus answered him:

Happy son of Laertes, Odysseus of many devices,
193	truly with great excellence you won your wife.
194	How good were the wits of blameless Penelope,
195	daughter of Icarius; how well she remembered Odysseus,
196	her wedded husband; therefore the fame of her
197	excellence will never perish, and the immortals will make
198	for those on earth a graceful song for prudent Penelope,
199	not as the daughter of Tyndareus devised evil deeds,
200	killing her wedded husband, and a hateful song
201	will be among men, and she will give a harsh report
202	to womankind, even to her who is virtuous.
So they spoke such things to one another,
standing in the house of Hades, beneath the depths of the earth.
And those, when they had come down from the city, soon reached the fair
farm of Laertes, well tended, which he himself
once won, since he toiled very much.
There was his house, and around it ran a lean-to on all sides,
in which the necessary servants, who worked for him with goodwill,
ate and sat and slept.
And there was a Sicilian woman, an old one, who
carefully tended the old man on the farm, away from the city.
There Odysseus spoke a word to the servants and his son:

You two go now into the well-built house,
215	and quickly sacrifice for dinner the best of the pigs;
216	but I shall make trial of our father,
217	whether he will recognise me and know me with his eyes,
218	or fail to know me, after being so long apart.
So saying he gave the servants the weapons of war.
They then went quickly to the house, but Odysseus
went nearer to the fruitful vineyard, making trial.
And he did not find Dolius, as he went down into the great orchard,
nor any of the servants nor of the sons; but they
had gone to gather stones for the fence of the vineyard
as a wall, and the old man led them on the way.
Him alone, his father, he found in the well-tended vineyard,
hoeing a plant; and he wore a dirty tunic,
patched and shabby, and about his shins he had bound
patched leggings of oxhide, to guard against scratches,
and gloves on his hands because of the brambles; and above
a goatskin cap he had on his head, nursing his grief.
And when the much-enduring godly Odysseus saw him
wasted with old age and having great grief in his heart,
standing under a tall pear tree he shed a tear.
Then he pondered in mind and spirit
whether to kiss and embrace his father, and tell each thing,
how he had come and reached his native land,
or first to question him and test each point.
And as he thought, this seemed to him the better course,
first to make trial of him with mocking words.
With this in mind godly Odysseus went straight up to him.
He, holding his head down, was digging round a plant;
and his shining son, standing by, spoke to him:

Old man, you lack no skill in tending
245	the orchard, but your care is good, and nothing at all,
246	no plant, no fig, no vine, no olive,
247	no pear, no garden-bed in the garden lacks care.
248	And another thing I shall tell you, and do not take anger in your heart:
249	you yourself are not well cared for, but with old age
250	you have woeful squalor and bad and unseemly clothes.
251	Surely your master does not neglect you for laziness,
252	nor is anything slavish seen in you to look at,
253	in form and stature; for you are like a kingly man.
254	You are like one who, when he has washed and eaten,
255	should sleep softly; for that is the right of old men.
256	But come, tell me this and relate it truly:
257	whose slave are you among men? and whose orchard do you tend?
258	And tell me this truly, that I may know well,
259	whether this is really Ithaca we have reached, as said to me
260	this man just now, meeting me as I came here,
261	not very sensible, since he did not dare to tell each thing
262	nor listen to my word, when I asked
263	about my guest-friend, whether he lives and is
264	or is already dead and in the house of Hades.
265	For I will tell you, and do you mark and listen to me:
266	a man I once entertained in my dear native land,
267	who came to our house, and no other mortal
268	of far-off dear strangers has come to my house;
269	he claimed to be of Ithaca by race, and said
270	that his father was Laertes, son of Arceisius.
271	Him I led to my house and entertained well,
272	cherishing him heartily, with much in the house,
273	and gave him guest-gifts, such as were fitting.
274	Of well-wrought gold I gave him seven talents,
275	and I gave him a mixing-bowl of solid silver, flowered,
276	twelve single cloaks, as many rugs,
277	as many fair mantles, and as many tunics besides,
278	and apart women too, who knew blameless works,
279	four fair ones, whom he himself wished to choose.
Then his father answered him, shedding tears:

Stranger, you have indeed come to the land you ask about,
282	but insolent and wanton men hold it;
283	and these gifts you bestowed, giving countless things, were in vain;
284	for if you had found him alive in the land of Ithaca,
285	he would have sent you off, repaying you well with gifts
286	and with good hospitality; for that is the right of whoever begins.
287	But come, tell me this and relate it truly:
288	how many years is it since you entertained that
289	guest of yours, ill-fated, my son, if ever he was,
290	ill-starred? whom somewhere far from friends and native land
291	either fish ate in the sea, or on dry land
292	he became prey to beasts and birds; and his mother
293	did not weep for him, laying him out, nor his father, who begot him;
294	nor his wife, rich in gifts, prudent Penelope,
295	wailed for her husband on the bed, as was fitting,
296	closing his eyes; for that is the due of the dead.
297	And tell me this truly, that I may know well:
298	Who are you among men, and whence? Where is your city and your parents?
299	Where is the swift ship moored, which brought you here
300	and your godlike comrades? Or have you come as a passenger
301	on another's ship, and they put you ashore and went?
Then answering him spoke Odysseus of many wiles:

Therefore I will tell you everything very truly.
304	I am from Alybas, where I live in a famous house,
305	son of Apheidas, son of lord Polypemon;
306	and my name is Eperitus; but a god
307	drove me from Sicania to come here against my will;
308	and my ship stands here by the farm, away from the city.
309	And for Odysseus this is now the fifth year,
310	since he went from there and left my country,
311	ill-fated; yet good were the birds for him as he went,
312	on the right, at which I rejoiced and sent him off,
313	and he rejoiced as he went; and our spirits still hoped
314	to meet in hospitality and to give splendid gifts.
So he spoke, and a black cloud of grief covered him;
and with both hands taking sooty dust
he poured it on his grey head, groaning heavily.
And Odysseus' spirit was stirred, and up his nostrils already
a sharp pang shot, as he looked at his dear father.
He leapt and embraced and kissed him, and said:

That man is I myself here, father, whom you ask about,
322	I have come in the twentieth year to my native land.
323	But hold from weeping and tearful lament.
324	For I will tell you; and we must hurry very much all the same:
325	I have killed the suitors in our house,
326	avenging their heart-grieving insult and evil deeds.
Then Laertes answered him and spoke:

If you are indeed Odysseus, my son, who have come here,
329	tell me now a clear sign, that I may be convinced.
Then answering him spoke Odysseus of many wiles:

First look with your eyes at this scar,
332	which on Parnassus a boar struck me with a white tusk
333	when I went; and you sent me and my lady mother
334	to my mother's dear father Autolycus, that I might take
335	the gifts which, coming here, he promised and nodded to me.
336	And come, I will tell you also the trees in the well-tended vineyard,
337	which you once gave me, and I asked you for each one,
338	a child, following you through the garden; and through them
339	we walked, and you named and told each one.
340	Pear trees you gave me thirteen and ten apple trees,
341	forty fig trees; and vines you named thus
342	you would give me fifty rows, each one of which
343	ripened at different times; and there were grapes of every kind on them—
344	whenever the seasons of Zeus pressed down from above.
So he spoke, and on the spot his knees and dear heart were loosened,
as he recognised the signs that Odysseus told him unerringly.
He threw his arms about his dear son; and the much-enduring
godly Odysseus drew him to himself as he fainted.
But when he breathed again and his spirit was gathered to his mind,
again he answered him and spoke:

Father Zeus, you gods still exist on long Olympus,
352	if truly the suitors have paid for their wanton insolence.
353	But now I am terribly afraid in my mind that soon all the men
354	of Ithaca will come here, and send messengers
355	everywhere to the cities of the Cephallenians.
Then answering him spoke Odysseus of many wiles:

Take courage, let not these things be a care in your mind.
358	But let us go to the house, which lies near the orchard;
359	there I sent ahead Telemachus and the cowherd and the swineherd,
360	to prepare dinner as quickly as possible.
So speaking the two went to the fair house.
And when they reached the well-inhabited house,
they found Telemachus and the cowherd and the swineherd
cutting much meat and mixing the gleaming wine.
Meanwhile great-hearted Laertes in his own house
the Sicilian handmaid bathed and anointed with oil,
and threw a fair cloak about him; and Athena
standing close by made the limbs of the shepherd of the people grow big,
and made him taller and stouter to look upon than before.
He came out of the bath; and his dear son marvelled at him,
when he saw him like the immortal gods face to face;
and speaking to him addressed him with winged words:

O father, truly one of the gods who live for ever
374	has made you better in form and stature to look at.
Then prudent Laertes answered him:

Would that, father Zeus and Athena and Apollo,
377	such as I was when I took Nericus, the well-built stronghold,
378	the headland of the mainland, ruling the Cephallenians,
379	such as that, yesterday in our house,
380	holding arms on my shoulders, I had stood and defended you
381	against the suitors; then I would have loosened the knees of many of them
382	in the halls, and you would have rejoiced in your mind within.
So they spoke such things to one another.
And the others, when they had ceased from toil and prepared the feast,
sat down in order on the stools and chairs;
there they set about the dinner, and near them
came old Dolius, and with him the sons of the old man,
worn out from work, for their mother had come out and called them,
the old Sicilian woman, who nursed them and tended the old man
carefully, since old age had seized him.
And they, when they saw Odysseus and perceived him in their hearts,
stood in the halls amazed; but Odysseus
addressed them with gentle words and said:
So he spoke, and Dolius went straight with both hands
stretched out, and taking Odysseus' hand he kissed it at the wrist,
and speaking to him addressed him with winged words:

Dear friend, since you have come home to us who longed for you greatly
401	and no longer expected it, and the gods themselves brought you back,
402	hail and be very glad, and may the gods give you blessings.
403	And tell me this truly, that I may know well:
404	whether wise Penelope already knows clearly
405	that you have come back here, or should we send a messenger?
Then answering him spoke Odysseus of many wiles:
Old man, she already knows; why must you trouble about this?
So he spoke, and he sat down again on the well-polished chair.
And in the same way the sons of Dolius around famous Odysseus
welcomed him with words and clung to his hands,
and sat down in order beside Dolius, their father.
So they were busy about the dinner in the halls;
and Rumour, a messenger, went quickly everywhere through the city,
telling of the hateful death and fate of the suitors.
And they, all alike hearing, came flocking from one place and another
with groaning and moaning before the house of Odysseus,
and carried the dead out of the houses and buried them, each his own,
and those from other cities they sent each to his home,
putting them on swift ships for fishermen to bring;
and themselves went to the assembly all together, grieved at heart.
And when they had gathered and were assembled,
among them Eupeithes stood up and spoke;
for unforgettable grief for his son lay in his mind,
Antinous, whom first godly Odysseus had killed;
for him shedding tears he made a speech and said:

Friends, truly this man has devised a great deed against the Achaeans;
427	some with ships he led away, many and good,
428	and lost the hollow ships, and lost the people;
429	and others on coming he killed, the best of the Cephallenians.
430	But come, before this man goes quickly to Pylos
431	or even to divine Elis, where the Epeians rule,
432	let us go; or else afterwards we shall be downcast always;
433	for this is a disgrace even for future men to hear,
434	if we do not take vengeance on the killers of our sons and brothers.
435	For me it would not be sweet in my mind
436	to live, but I would rather die soonest and be among the dead.
437	But let us go, lest they cross over and forestall us.
So he spoke weeping, and pity seized all the Achaeans.
And near them came Medon and the godly singer
from the halls of Odysseus, when sleep had released them,
and stood in the midst; and wonder seized each man.
And among them spoke Medon, knowing wise things:

Hear me now, men of Ithaca; for Odysseus
444	did not devise these deeds without the will of the immortal gods;
445	I myself saw an immortal god, who stood
446	near Odysseus and was like Mentor in everything.
447	The immortal god now before Odysseus
448	appeared, giving him courage, and now rousing the suitors
449	rushed through the hall; and they fell thick one by one.
So he spoke, and pale fear seized them all.
And among them spoke the old hero Halitherses,
son of Mastor; for he alone saw before and after;
he, thinking well for them, made a speech and said:

Hear me now, men of Ithaca, what I shall say:
455	by your own wickedness, friends, these deeds came about;
456	for you did not obey me, nor Mentor, shepherd of the people,
457	to stop your sons from their follies,
458	who did a great deed by evil wantonness,
459	wasting the possessions and dishonouring the wife
460	of a noble man; and they said he would no longer return.
461	And now let it be so. Obey me as I say:
462	let us not go, lest someone find a self-drawn evil.
So he spoke, and they sprang up with a great shout,
more than half; and the others stayed there together;
for this speech did not please them in their minds, but they obeyed
Eupeithes; and at once they hurried to their arms.
And when they had put the gleaming bronze about their bodies,
they gathered together before the wide-spaced town.
And Eupeithes led them in his folly;
he said he would avenge his son's death, but he was not to
return back, but to meet his doom there.
And Athena spoke to Zeus the son of Kronos:

O our father, son of Kronos, highest of rulers,
474	tell me, who ask, what does your mind hide within?
475	Will you further make evil war and dread battle,
476	or will you put friendship between both sides?
Then answering her spoke Zeus the cloud-gatherer:

My child, why do you ask and enquire of me this?
479	Did you not yourself plan this design,
480	that Odysseus should come and punish those men?
481	Do as you wish; and I shall tell you what is fitting.
482	Since godly Odysseus has punished the suitors,
483	let them make sure oaths, and let him be king always,
484	and let us bring about forgetfulness of the slaughter
485	of sons and brothers; and let them love one another
486	as before, and let wealth and peace be abundant.
So saying he urged Athena, who was eager before,
and she went darting down from the peaks of Olympus.
And they, when they had put away the desire for honey-sweet food,
among them began to speak the much-enduring godly Odysseus:
Let someone go out and see lest they are coming near.
So he spoke; and the son of Dolius went out, as he bade;
he went and stood on the threshold, and saw them all near;
and at once he addressed Odysseus with winged words:
They are close at hand; but let us arm quickly.
So he spoke, and they rose and put on their arms,
four with Odysseus, and six sons of Dolius;
and Laertes and Dolius too put on their arms,
grey-haired though they were, warriors of necessity.
And when they had put the gleaming bronze about their bodies,
they opened the doors and went out, and Odysseus led.
And near them came Athena, daughter of Zeus,
likened to Mentor both in form and voice.
Seeing her the much-enduring godly Odysseus rejoiced;
and at once he spoke to Telemachus, his dear son:

Telemachus, now you will know this yourself, coming
507	where men fight and the best are decided,
508	not to shame the race of your fathers, who in the past
509	have excelled in valour and manliness over all the earth.
Then prudent Telemachus answered him:

You will see, if you wish, dear father, in this spirit of mine
512	that I do not at all shame your race, as you say.
So he spoke, and Laertes rejoiced and said a word:

What a day is this for me, dear gods! Truly I rejoice;
515	son and grandson contend about excellence.
And standing by him spoke grey-eyed Athena:

O son of Arceisius, far the dearest of all comrades,
518	pray to the grey-eyed maiden and to father Zeus,
519	and quickly poising it hurl your long-shadowed spear.
So spoke Pallas Athena, and breathed great strength into him.
And praying then to the daughter of great Zeus,
he quickly poised and hurled his long-shadowed spear,
and hit Eupeithes through his bronze-cheeked helmet.
It did not hold off the spear, and the bronze went straight through,
and he fell with a thud, and his armour clanged upon him.
And Odysseus and his shining son fell upon the foremost fighters,
and struck them with swords and double-pointed spears.
And now they would have killed them all and made them without return,
had not Athena, daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus,
cried out with her voice, and held back all the people:

Hold from grievous war, men of Ithaca,
532	that you may be parted quickly without bloodshed.
So spoke Athena, and pale fear seized them;
and in their fear their arms flew from their hands,
and all fell to the ground, as the goddess uttered her voice;
and they turned toward the city, longing for life.
And terribly shouted the much-enduring godly Odysseus,
and swooped, gathered himself, like a high-flying eagle.
And then the son of Kronos sent down a smoking thunderbolt,
and it fell before the grey-eyed daughter of the mighty father.
Then grey-eyed Athena spoke to Odysseus:

Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus of many devices,
543	hold, and stop the strife of even war,
544	lest somehow Zeus the son of Kronos, far-sounding, be angry with you.
So spoke Athena, and he obeyed, and rejoiced in spirit.
And afterwards oaths for both sides she set,
Pallas Athena, daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus,
likened to Mentor both in form and voice.
